subject: Accounting
title: Tax Credits vs. Deductions
description: One-minute skill: Tax Credits vs. Deductions.

hook.text: A $1,000 deduction saves you maybe $220. A $1,000 credit saves you exactly $1,000.

buildup.text: Deductions lower the income you're taxed on. Credits directly reduce the tax you owe.

discovery.text: The child tax credit, education credits, and energy credits are common dollar-for-dollar savings.

twist.text: Some credits are refundable—meaning you get cash back even if you owe zero tax.

climax.text: Smart tax planning prioritizes credits over deductions because credits have more impact.

punchline.text: Credits beat deductions. Dollar for dollar, no contest.

quiz.question: How does a tax credit differ from a deduction?
options: Credits directly reduce tax owed; deductions reduce taxable income

details.summary: Tax credits reduce your tax bill dollar-for-dollar while deductions only reduce your taxable income, making credits significantly more valuable. A $1,000 credit saves you $1,000; a $1,000 deduction may only save you $220.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding the difference between credits and deductions is crucial for tax planning because credits provide far more tax savings per dollar, and many people miss valuable credits they qualify for.
takeaways: Tax credits directly reduce your tax bill by the credit amount, dollar for dollar
Tax deductions only reduce the income on which tax is calculated, providing smaller savings
Some credits are refundable meaning they can create a refund even if you owe no tax

faq.question: What is the difference between a tax credit and a tax deduction?
faq.answer: A tax credit directly reduces your tax bill — a $1,000 credit means you pay $1,000 less in tax. A deduction reduces your taxable income — a $1,000 deduction in the 22% bracket only saves you $220. Credits are always more valuable dollar-for-dollar than deductions.

faq.question: What is a refundable tax credit?
faq.answer: A refundable credit pays you back even if it exceeds what you owe. If you owe $500 in tax but have a $2,000 refundable credit, you get a $1,500 refund. Non-refundable credits can only reduce your tax to zero. The Earned Income Tax Credit and parts of the Child Tax Credit are refundable.
